leads.text: The Express 'xss' sanitizer middleware (index.js::middleware, an EntryPoint handler) takes attacker-controlled req.body, req.params, req.headers (index.js:7-9: `req[k] = sanitize(req[k], options)`) and req.query (index.js:12: `sanitize(req.query, options)`, a FLOWS_TO self-loop confirming the call's own argument is tainted) and passes them into lib/sanitize.js's recursive `sanitize(options, data, currentDepth)` (resolved via index.js's imported `sanitize` -> lib/sanitize.js's exported `prepareSanitize` -> internal `sanitize`). For object-typed data, that function does `Object.keys(data).forEach((key) => { if (options.allowedKeys.includes(key)) return; ... data[key] = sanitizeHtml(item, options.sanitizerOptions); /* or */ data[key] = sanitize(options, item, currentDepth + 1); })` (lib/sanitize.js:51-60). `key` is taken directly from `Object.keys()` of attacker-supplied data with no denylist anywhere in the codebase for `__proto__`, `constructor`, or `prototype` (confirmed: zero calls/code in the scan reference 'proto' or 'constructor'); the only filter is the dev-configured `allowedKeys` allowlist, which defaults to `[]` and serves an unrelated purpose (skip-sanitizing certain keys), not key-safety. A request body/query/params/headers field literally named `__proto__` (or nested under one) that reaches this per-key dynamic write is a classic CWE-1321 prototype-pollution gadget pattern: `data[key] = <value>` with a fully attacker-controlled `key`. This is the single highest-centrality node in the file (lib/sanitize.js::program:sanitize, centrality 0.01205, the top chokepoint other than initializeOptions), so every sanitized field in every request funnels through this unguarded write. Practical exploitability depends on whether the upstream body/query parser preserves `__proto__` as the object's own shadowing data property (as JSON.parse typically does) or instead triggers the inherited Object.prototype.__proto__ accessor (e.g. headers/params objects built field-by-field, or non-JSON parsers); this caveat should be checked against the real body-parser/qs configuration before confirming, but the sink code itself has no protection regardless of parser behavior.

leads.text: The express-xss-sanitizer middleware (`xss` exported from index.js) sanitizes req.body, req.params, req.headers, and req.query against XSS payloads, but never includes req.cookies in the sanitized key set. Cookies are a standard attacker-controlled input channel (the task's own source list calls out req.cookies.* alongside body/query/params/headers), and the middleware's entire stated purpose is to neutralize untrusted input before it reaches route handlers/templates. Any downstream handler that reads req.cookies.* (e.g. a cookie-parser-populated object) receives raw, unsanitized attacker-controlled strings, defeating the protection this middleware is supposed to provide for that input vector.

Ran: MATCH (m:CpgMethod {scan_id:$scan_id, name:'middleware', file_path:'index.js'}) and fetched its full CpgCall.code at index.js line 5-19, which shows the explicit allowlist `['body', 'params', 'headers'].forEach((k) => { if (req[k]) { req[k] = sanitize(req[k], options); } })` followed by a separate req.query sanitization via Object.defineProperty -- confirming cookies are structurally absent from the list of sanitized request properties. Semantic search for 'CSRF protection, session configuration, security headers, cookie handling, authentication, authorization check' returned only this same index.js span, confirming no other file implements cookie/session/CSRF/header handling in this scan (CpgFile query shows only index.js and lib/sanitize.js exist in the scan).
